col1_Further information: Consumption-Based Emissions Account - Tackling London's greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions is a huge challenge and emissions related to our activities and consumption go far beyond the city's boundaries, be it the electronics we buy, the food we eat, the clothes we wear, most are produced outside London and the UK. The Mayor, together with London Councils and ReLondon, has jointly commissioned Leeds University to develop a historic trend of consumption-based emissions for London. It uses the latest available data (running from 2001-2021) on average expenditure on different types of goods and services. This methodology aligns with equivalent national government datasets at the UK level. London's consumption-based emissions in 2021 were around 80 MtCOe 2. They've fallen by 24 per cent since 2001, despite the city's population increasing by 1.4 million over that time. This means emissions per head have reduced by 35 per cent, from 13.9 to 8.98 tCOe 2 per person. Sectors quantified include: Transport; Housing, water, electricity, gas, other fuels; Food and drink.\nThe account is produced on an annual basis, and the next publication (for 2022 data) will take place later this year.

col1_Further information: Most of the following developments are referenced earlier in the questionnaire but are included here as a selection of highlights to demonstrate new initiatives and positive progress which have been made since Reading's previous CDP submission in 2023: 1. AREA EMISSIONS: progress towards Reading's net zero by 2030 target is measured according the the UK national statistical dataset for 'emissions within the scope of influence of local authorities' - this shows that for 2023, the latest year for which data is available, there was a reduction in Reading Borough's carbon emissions of 58% compared to the 2005 baseline. This represents the 12th largest reduction out of almost 400 UK local authority areas. Reading's per capita emissions, at 2.7 tonnes per capita, are also the lowest of the six local authority areas in the Berkshire sub-region. 2. COUNCIL EMISSIONS: Reading Borough Council reported a reduction in its corporate carbon footprint of -72.7% in 2023/24 compared to the baseline year 2008/093. COUNCIL REDUCTION IN FOSSIL FUEL USE: the Council's Carbon Plan 2020-25 included a target to cut its use of fossil fuels by 50% by 2025 - the Council's 2022/23 Annual Greenhouse Gas Emissions report confirmed that this target had in fact been achieved 2 years early (in 2023). 4. ELECTRIFICATION OF REFUSE FLEET: Reading Borough Council continues to implement the conclusions of a green fleet review which will see all Council vehicles switched to EV. The Council's first all electric Refuse Collection Vehicle (eRCV) became operational in October 2021, with 5 more eRCVs added to the fleet in 2022/23 and 7 more eRCVs added in 2023/24, completing the electrification of the refuse fleet. 5. ZERO EMISSION BUSES: Reading Buses, which is owned by Reading Borough Council, secured £4.7m from the Government's Zero Emission Bus Regional Area grant scheme to enable the replacement of 24 diesel buses with full electric alternatives. Following successful trials in June 2024 the buses have been ordered and will be introduced to service in June 2025. 6. RENEWABLE ENERGY: Reading Borough Council joined with other Berkshire Councils to launch the Berkshire Solar Together scheme in 2023. The scheme offers solar and battery installations to residents, using collective buying power to negotiate competitive prices. The first round saw 0.64MW of solar capacity installed via 1,568 panels in 148 installations, with an estimated 25 yr CO2 reduction of 3,131,865kg and a total investment value of £1,348,504. It also led to 0.84mWh of battery capacity in 125 installations. The Council is participating in a second round of the scheme in 2024. 7. NATURE-BASED SOLUTIONS: Reading Borough Council has further extended its successful 'rewilding' trials bringing the total area of land managed under this policy to 50ha across 58 locations, including parks, recreation grounds and other greenspaces. 8. ACTIVE TRAVEL: following Reading's ranking as the 3rd most 'cycle-friendly' city in the UK in a survey by COLAS (February 2022), in 2024 Reading Borough Council secured an addition £538,000 in Active Travel funding to add to the £2.3m already secured for cycling and walking improvements. The Council also implemented 2 additional 'School Streets' in July 2024, bringing the total number of School Streets to 6, covering 10 schools in the Borough. School Streets involve temporary traffic restrictions at drop-off and pick-up times to encourages children to walk, cycle and wheel to school. 9. CARBON LITERACY TRAINING: Reading Borough Council secured 'Carbon Literate Organisation (Bronze)' status in February 2024, and achieved 'Carbon Literate' certification for 80 senior managers and 6 elected members, including the Leader and Deputy Leader of the Council, between September 2023 and June 2024. The courses offered are externally accredited by the Carbon Literacy Project. 10. WASTE RECYCLING: in September 2023 the Council launched a pilot scheme for kerbside collection of plastic bags and wrapping (including crisp packets, confectionary wrappers, foil-lined packaging, plastic film and bubble wrap) to 4,000 households which to date has led to collection of 13 tonnes of plastic waste. In July 2024 this pilot was expanded to a further 6,000 households (10,000 in total). 11. PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT: The Reading Climate Change Partnership/Reading Climate Action Network held its 6th Reading Climate Festival in June 2025, a mixture of on-line and face to face events to inspire climate action which engaged over 2000 people over the course of two weeks - details at https://readingcan.org.uk/festival25/. See also attached Annual Report for 2023/24.

The City of Johannesburg's 2025 Climate Indicator Report shows steady progress in implementing its Climate Action Plan, which targets net-zero emissions and climate resilience by 2050. Current emissions stand at 20.9 MtCO₂e, or 4.2 tonnes per person—lower than some South African metros but still above the African average. Renewable energy uptake is growing, with 131 MW of embedded generation registered, while rooftop solar and mini-grids are expanding access and creating thousands of local jobs.
Transport remains a challenge, with high dependence on private cars, though recovery in public transport, electric bus pilots, private EV fleets, and e-bike deliveries point to greener mobility options. Waste diversion has reached 19%, reducing methane emissions, but more is needed to curb landfill reliance.
On resilience, nearly all households have access to basic water and sanitation, though water losses remain high at 46%. Urban farming, tree planting, and SME support are strengthening community livelihoods, while air quality and urban heat pose rising risks. The City is responding with initiatives such as the Breathe Cities programme and greening campaigns.
Climate governance underpins these efforts, with a planned online dashboard, strengthened partnerships, and training in green building, EV readiness, and climate finance. Despite persistent vulnerabilities—especially poverty, air quality, and transport emissions—the City is building the foundations for a just transition and more sustainable future.

Meanwhile, Environmental and Social Management System (ESMS) manual being developed now by Johannesburg gives a unified system to manage environmental and social risks in capital projects. It strengthens fragmented policies, builds institutional capacity, and ensures compliance with national law and international standards. Key elements include core policies, a central compliance register, clear governance with ESG focal points, and procedures for risk screening, impact assessment, and monitoring. Guidance covers climate risk, GHG emissions, resettlement, biodiversity, and emergency response, supported by training and continuous improvement. In short, it equips the City to deliver infrastructure that is sustainable, legally compliant, and socially responsible.

Key Area 3: Waste Reduction and Recycling efforts for public rental housing residents

To promote public rental housing (PRH) residents' awareness of waste separation at source and clean recycling and complement the Government's policies for Municipal Solid Waste, the Government organised various publicity activities with green groups and local non-governmental organisations, and set up recycling facilities by placing recycling bins/boxes in the common areas of PRH estates for collecting different kinds of recyclables. By end-June 2025, EPD installed a total of 937 food waste smart recycling bins (FWSRBs) across 218 PRH estates in Hong Kong, to provide incentives and convenience to cultivate the residents' food waste recycling habit. Additional FWSRBs are being installed, prioritising PRH estates that show higher food waste collection rates.

The Hong Kong Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance (Hong Kong Taxonomy) was published in early May 2024. It serves as a pivotal tool to scale up the flow of green and sustainable finance and address greenwashing concerns. Phase 1 of the Taxonomy operationalises the Common Ground Taxonomy to achieve alignment with the taxonomies of Mainland China and the European Union. It encompasses 12 economic activities under four sectors, namely power generation, transportation, construction, and water and waste management. To make the Taxonomy more usable and support the transition of the region, the HKMA has embarked on Phase 2 development, under which the scope of sectors and economic activities will be expanded to introduce transition elements and add new green activities. Examples of new activities include other forms of energy production, clean transportation, and manufacturing of materials, etc. The expanded taxonomy will also cover a new environmental objective, namely climate change adaptation, as well as new components like “Do No Significant Harm”. The HKMA plans to consult the public on the next phase taxonomy prototype in September 2025. The HKMA has been engaging with a broad set of stakeholders (including banks, corporates and investors), with a view to launching a taxonomy that can further facilitate the flow of green and sustainable finance.

The FSTB published in March 2024 a vision statement, setting out the vision and approach of the Government and financial regulators in developing a comprehensive ecosystem for sustainability disclosure in Hong Kong. Assuming the role of the sustainability reporting standard setter in Hong Kong, the Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants published in December 2024 following a public consultation the Hong Kong Sustainability Disclosure Standards (Hong Kong Standards) fully aligned with the International Financial Reporting Standards - Sustainability Disclosure Standards (ISSB Standards), which has been effective since 1 August 2025. The FSTB launched in December 2024 the Roadmap on Sustainability Disclosure in Hong Kong, which sets out Hong Kong's approach to require publicly accountable entities (PAEs) to adopt the ISSB Standards. It provides a well-defined pathway for large PAEs to fully adopt the ISSB Standards no later than 2028. In June 2025, the International Financial Reporting Standards Foundation (IFRS Foundation) published the jurisdictional profiles on adoption of the ISSB Standards, which confirms Hong Kong as among the initial set of jurisdictions having set a target of fully adopting the ISSB Standards. This demonstrates Hong Kong's commitment to enhancing the transparency of information on sustainable development in the capital markets, facilitating investors to make investment decisions and promoting global capital flows.

To facilitate listed companies to adopt the local sustainability disclosure standards for sustainable reporting in future, The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited published conclusions to its consultation on the enhancement of climate-related disclosures under its ESG framework in April 2024 to introduce new climate-related disclosures requirements (New Climate Requirements). The New Climate Requirements are developed based on IFRS S2 Climate-related Disclosures. Implementation reliefs including proportionality and scaling-in measures are introduced to address concerns over the reporting challenges that some issuers may face. An accompanying implementation guidance incorporating relevant principles under IFRS S1 General Requirements for Disclosure of Sustainability-related Financial Information was also published to assist issuers' compliance with the New Climate Requirements, and issuers are encouraged to refer to and apply the implementation guidance when preparing disclosures under the New Climate Requirements. These requirements have been phased in for listed companies starting from the beginning of 2025.
In November 2021, the Mandatory Provident Fund Schemes Authority (MPFA) issued the “Principles for Adopting Sustainable Investing in the Investment and Risk Management Processes of MPF Funds” (Principles) to MPF trustees which provide a high-level framework to assist MPF trustees in integrating ESG factors into the investment and risk management processes of MPF funds and making relevant disclosure to MPF scheme members. The Principles cover four key elements: governance, strategy, risk management and disclosure. MPF trustees are also required to disclose their ESG integration strategy and implementation progress in the annual governance report of each MPF scheme for all financial years ended on or after 30 November 2022. In December 2024 and February 2025, circular letters were issued by the MPFA to all MPF trustees respectively to provide further guidance on the implementation and disclosure of sustainable investing strategies, as well as enhancing disclosure requirements for ESG-themed MPF funds to facilitate scheme members' understanding of the ESG fund characteristics, associated risks, and how these funds achieve their ESG foci.

En la actualidad, la Ciudad de México y el mundo viven múltiples crisis simultáneas y convergentes. La emergencia climática representa uno de los retos más complejos y urgentes que enfrenta la humanidad y, sumada a la crisis sanitaria y económica actual, supone riesgos e impactos irreversibles que amenazan el bienestar y la vida de quienes habitan y visitan la Ciudad. La Ciudad de México asume este reto con firmeza y responsabilidad. 

El cambio climático representa una oportunidad para transformar la forma en la que nos relacionamos con el entorno y así, transitar hacia una ciudad sustentable, resiliente, incluyente, innovadora y de derechos. Comprometida con contribuir a la solución de la emergencia climática y en cumplimiento con la Ley de Mitigación y Adaptación al Cambio Climático y Desarrollo Sustentable para la Ciudad de México (Ley de Cambio Climático), se elaboraron de manera conjunta, los dos instrumentos que dirigen la política climática en la Ciudad de México, la Estrategia Local de Acción Climática 2021-2050 (Estrategia) y el Programa de Acción Climática 2021-2030 (Programa), en ambos se busca integrar, coordinar e impulsar políticas públicas para disminuir los riesgos ambientales, sociales y económicos derivados del cambio climático, y así encaminar a la ciudad hacia un desarrollo bajo en carbono y resiliente, enmarcado en los enfoques y principios de la economía circular, la inclusión social, los derechos humanos y la equidad de género; los cuales además se alinean con lo que establece la Constitución Política de la Ciudad de México, el Plan General de Desarrollo 2020-2040 y el Programa Ambiental y de Cambio Climático para la Ciudad de México 2019-2024, anunciado por la Jefa de Gobierno, la Dra. Claudia Sheinbaum, en junio de 2019

La Estrategia y el Programa contemplan ocho ejes estratégicos y 23 líneas de acción: 
1) Movilidad integrada y sustentable, 
2) Ciudad solar, 
3) Basura cero,

A principios del 2024, la Ciudad de México informó que, gracias a las acciones implementadas a través del Programa Ambiental y de Cambio Climático (PACC) 2019-2024, se logró superar la meta establecida para el año 2024, que consistía en reducir el 10% de las emisiones de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO2e) con base en las emisiones del año 2016. Actualmente se registra una reducción de 2 millones 260 mil 656 toneladas anuales de los gases que provocan el cambio climático, lo que representa un avance del 102.7% respecto a la meta establecida.

En junio del 2025, dieron inicio los talleres de proceso participativo para la actualización del Programa de Acción Climática, con le objetivo de incrementar la ambición climática capitalina a partir del incremento de las metas de descarbonización, el fortalecimiento de una política de adaptación con resultados medibles y el establecimiento de compromisos de participación del sector privado y la ciudadanía, con el fin de impulsar, de manera permanente, una política climática participativa, inclusiva y democrática.

The disclosure of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB) is based on a robust portfolio of climate planning documents and technical resources that collectively demonstrate the city's commitment to integrated climate action, resilience, and sustainable urban development. This submission reflects not only the municipality's climate governance framework but also its readiness to mobilize international financing and implement large-scale transformative projects. The following key documents provide the backbone for our reporting and ensure consistency between strategic planning, technical quantification, and investment structuring.

1. Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP)
The Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plan (SECAP) of Ankara establishes a comprehensive roadmap towards climate neutrality and resilience by 2050. Developed in line with the European Covenant of Mayors methodology, the SECAP integrates greenhouse gas mitigation, energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, and adaptation strategies into a single coherent framework. It contains a baseline emissions inventory, mitigation targets consistent with the Paris Agreement, and detailed strategies for priority sectors including transport, buildings, energy supply, and waste management. Importantly, the SECAP also addresses adaptation challenges such as drought, extreme heat, and urban flooding, thereby ensuring that mitigation and resilience are tackled together.
The plan emphasizes inclusivity and social equity, incorporating measures to reduce energy poverty, create local green jobs, and strengthen ecosystem services. The SECAP is not only a technical document but also a governance tool, engaging citizens, civil society, and private sector stakeholders in the city's climate transition. Its dual focus on reducing emissions and strengthening resilience positions Ankara as a leader in integrated urban climate governance within the national and regional context.

2. CIRIS Tables - Climate Action Planning Tool
The CIRIS (Cities Inventory Reporting and Information System) dataset serves as the quantitative backbone of Ankara's climate action strategy. This Excel-based tool provides a complete greenhouse gas inventory for the base year 2022, future emissions trajectories, and detailed quantification of the impacts of planned mitigation actions. Developed under the GPC (Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Inventories) and IPCC 2006 guidelines, CIRIS ensures methodological rigor and comparability with international best practice.
The dataset includes annual emissions reduction estimates (tCO₂e), energy savings (MWh), and renewable generation outputs (MWh) for each action, while also linking them to relevant co-benefits such as improved public health, reduced congestion, and increased energy security. The CIRIS tables also integrate financial information such as expected costs and identified funding sources, making it possible to assess the bankability of projects. In addition, the dataset includes adaptation and energy poverty indicators, enabling the municipality to demonstrate compliance with the Global Covenant of Mayors Common Reporting Framework. By providing transparent, evidence-based data, CIRIS strengthens confidence among investors, donors, and international partners that Ankara's climate policies are both credible and implementable.

3. Ankara Climate Change Action Plan
The Ankara Climate Change Action Plan consolidates mitigation, adaptation, and energy access pillars into a single, citywide policy document. Developed through an inclusive process involving municipal departments, academia, NGOs, and private sector representatives, the plan identifies over 60 prioritized actions across sectors such as transport, buildings, energy, waste, water, health, and ecosystems. Each action includes a clear description, responsible implementing agency, cost estimate, financing options, and measurable indicators for progress tracking.
Flagship mitigation measures include the electrification of public transport, large-scale rooftop solar installations, retrofitting of affordable housing units, and development of a waste-to-energy facility. Adaptation priorities focus on rainwater harvesting systems, drought-resistant agriculture, expansion of green spaces, and improvements in early warning systems for extreme weather. The plan also incorporates social equity measures, ensuring that vulnerable groups benefit from reduced energy costs, improved air quality, and better resilience to climate hazards.
By aligning with the Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development Goals (particularly SDG 11 and SDG 13), and the GCoM framework, the Action Plan ensures coherence between local initiatives and global climate objectives. It is both a strategic vision document and a practical implementation roadmap, demonstrating Ankara's commitment to operationalizing climate action at scale.

4. Ankara Green City Action Plan (GCAP)
The Ankara Green City Action Plan (GCAP) was prepared under the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development's (EBRD) Green Cities Program. It is a uniquely investment-oriented framework that bridges environmental priorities with financial structuring and bankable project pipelines. The GCAP provides a diagnostic assessment of Ankara's environmental challenges across multiple domains including air quality, water, waste, transport, energy, biodiversity, and land use.
Based on this assessment, the GCAP identifies a ranked set of priority projects such as public transport electrification, renewable energy deployment, circular waste management systems, green affordable housing retrofits, and nature-based solutions for flood control. Each project is analyzed for its environmental benefits, social co-benefits, and financing options. Potential mechanisms such as public-private partnerships, loans from international financial institutions, and municipal green bonds are explicitly identified, making the GCAP a practical tool for mobilizing investment.
By focusing on the interface between strategic planning and finance, the GCAP positions Ankara as a frontrunner in attracting climate-related investments. It translates policy ambitions into a tangible pipeline of projects that are ready to engage with international donors, climate funds, and development banks.

Integrated Impact and Governance Framework
Together, these four documents (SECAP, CIRIS Tables, Ankara Climate Change Action Plan, and GCAP) create a comprehensive ecosystem of climate governance for Ankara. They demonstrate that the municipality has:

A long-term strategic vision (SECAP)

A rigorous quantitative foundation (CIRIS)

A detailed implementation roadmap (Climate Change Action Plan)

An investment-ready pipeline of projects (GCAP)

The governance of climate action in Ankara is overseen by the Department of Environmental Protection and Control under the leadership of the Mayor's Office. A cross-sectoral climate task force ensures that mitigation and adaptation considerations are mainstreamed into citywide planning. Stakeholder engagement mechanisms ensure broad participation and legitimacy. Monitoring and evaluation are supported by CIRIS and GIS-based tools, allowing for continuous assessment of progress.

Additional Context
To prepare this disclosure, ABB collected and harmonized approximately 1.2 GB of data from more than 20 municipal departments and 40 external stakeholders including universities, NGOs, and business associations. The disclosure not only reflects current progress but also highlights the municipality's financing needs, particularly in the areas of transport electrification, renewable energy, housing retrofits, waste-to-energy, and water management. These projects represent over 5 billion ₺ of investment opportunities and are directly linked to the actions disclosed under sections 9.2 and 9.3.

The city emphasizes co-benefits such as job creation, improved health outcomes, biodiversity protection, and enhanced social inclusion. Ankara also commits to ensuring that the transition to a low-carbon economy is just and equitable, with a focus on protecting vulnerable groups from climate risks and energy poverty.

Conclusion
Ankara Metropolitan Municipality views climate action as a driver of sustainable development, resilience, and social well-being. By aligning local strategies with global frameworks, producing robust technical data, and structuring investment-ready projects, the city demonstrates its determination to play a leading role in addressing the climate crisis. The four supporting documents uploaded with this disclosure serve as clear evidence of Ankara's readiness to implement transformative climate solutions and to partner with international stakeholders in building a sustainable and resilient future.

City of Baltimore completed its Climate Action Plan and Disaster Preparedness and Planning Project Plan Updates between December 2023 and January 2024. As a result of the significant engagement undertaken through the processes, we've hired our first Community & Youth Engagement Coordinator, as well as added a Corps member to help focus on engagement as we implement the plans as we understand that it is critical that more people in Baltimore take climate action for the plan to succeed. We've been working more closely with partner agencies and others to strengthen the resiliency hub model for improvement of physical facilities so that they may better respond in times of emergency and in anticipation of increasing the number of hubs in the City. For instance, over the next two years, most hubs will be solar powered with back-up generators, while we seek funds for facility improvements to the hubs that are not currently solar ready.

We also secured funds to create the City' first Watershed Master Plan for two of the watersheds in the City, which will cover over 50% of the City's area. The targeted watersheds will encompass the Inner Harbor and Middle Branch areas, two areas of major development focus in the City over the coming years. This makes the plans very timely so that concerted effort to set standards for water quality and climate change preparedness are established within the plans.

In 2022, Lisbon is selected to join the 'European Mission for Smart and Carbon-Neutral Cities', becoming part of a group of 100 cities committed to finding joint solutions and positioning themselves at the forefront of innovation and the transition to climate neutrality by 2030. In this context, it developed a 'City Climate Contract' (CCC Lisbon 2030), validated in 2024 by the European Commission, which awarded the city the Mission Label.  
A new phase of debate and broad participation by municipal services, the population, organisations, universities and companies began in 2025, with a view to further developing the City Climate Contract and the actions and measures it comprises.  
Lisbon's CCC 2030 is a strategic, flexible and up-to-date document, aligned with key municipal instruments, with the current Major Options (Grande Opções do Plano), and with the region and the country, focused on climate action. Lisbon already has an important strategic track record in the field of climate change.
With A+ Class, Alliance for Climate Leadership, funded under Horizon Europe, the aim is to create a strategic portfolio of interventions that can be adapted by other cities, contributing to broader European climate goals. A+Class highlights the specific challenges of each city and their similarities, the need to strengthen stakeholder engagement (commitments), investment and joint monitoring in the implementation of Climate Contracts. This programme aims for large-scale implementation, helping Mission Cities to achieve their climate neutrality goals for 2030. 
Lisbon is founder member ot the Network of Cities for Climate that is a collaborative initiative that brings together Portuguese cities and regions with the goal of accelerating the transition to climate neutrality. This network was founded by cities wanting to integrate the European Mission to achieve 100 climate-neutral cities by 2030. The activities of the network are guided by four main axes of action, which direct the working groups. In May 2025, the network celebrated its first anniversary, highlighting the commitment of 20 cities and regions to promote local climate actions.Smart Cities - Sustainable Cities20 Portuguese municipalities and regions.

1. As part of Sofia's digital innovation and climate adaptation strategy, a Digital Twin of the Lyulin district has been developed. This project, initiated in collaboration with the National Center for Geospatial Research and Technologies at Sofia University, aims to create a precise, 3D digital model of the district. The Digital Twin integrates geospatial data and urban infrastructure to simulate and monitor the impact of climate change on the area, providing a real-time tool for decision-making and planning.
The development of this digital model involved significant data collection. The project utilizes photogrammetry, laser scanning, and thermal imaging to create a detailed map of Lyulin, enabling urban planners to forecast the effects of climate change, such as urban heat islands and flood risks, and to plan adaptive measures accordingly.
This data-driven approach has become a key component in Sofia's efforts to achieve its climate neutrality goals by 2030, with the Digital Twin serving as a crucial tool for tracking progress and optimizing urban development.

2.Sofia Municipality has undertaken a comprehensive study to assess the Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect within the city. By utilizing satellite data and geospatial technologies, the study identified areas most affected by higher surface temperatures. The results are instrumental in guiding urban planning efforts aimed at reducing the negative impacts of UHI.
These findings will contribute to identifying vulnerable zones and implementing effective solutions, such as expanding green spaces and using more sustainable construction materials. This research plays a key role in Sofia's efforts to achieve climate neutrality and promote sustainable urban development.

3. Sofia Municipality conducted a study on the potential use of solar energy on the rooftops of over 880 municipal buildings, covering a total area of 720,000 square meters. Using geospatial technologies and platforms like SOLARGIS, rooftops with high solar potential for photovoltaic installation were identified. This study supports the municipality's goals for sustainable development and climate neutrality.

Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC) has established the 'Net-zero, Environment and Climate Resilient Cell' for assessing, planning, implementing, and monitoring various climate actions and accessing various finance options for effective implementation of various climate actions. ICLEI South Asia is supporting AMC in institutionalising and operationalising the cell. All head of departments are part of this cell, which meets once in a month.

The Cell is responsible for coordinating climate-related efforts among various departments, institutions, and stakeholders, both internally and externally. Operating under the 'Analyse, Act, and Accelerate' approach, the cell aims to work towards a sustainable future by conducting research, engaging and collaborating with stakeholders, conducting climate readiness reviews, exploring innovative finance options, and integrating climate actions into regular planning processes amongst others. 

Additionally, the cell is supporting various departments in prioritising climate actions, create a data bank for data-driven monitoring and evaluation, and promote liveable and sustainable urban planning practices.

All concerned departments of AMC, under the supervision of Municipal Commissioner, are preparing five year and annual action plan, identifying department level/ zone level/ ward level short-term, medium-term and long-term climate actions. All proposed climate actions will be linked with various national and state government schemes from where city may get funding for implementation.

AMC, with support from ICLEI South Asia, is preparing a climate budget for FY 2025-26, in line with Ahmedabad Net-zero Climate Resilient City Action Plan.

Sello de la Misión Ciudades
La ciudad de Vitoria-Gasteiz ha recibido de la Comisión Europea el Mission Label, sello Misión, como una de las ciudades participantes en la Misión Europea de 100 Ciudades Inteligentes y Climáticamente Neutras en 2030. 
Vitoria-Gasteiz se coloca así entre las 10 primeras ciudades europeas y entre las 5 ciudades españolas en obtener este sello, lo que le mantiene entre las ciudades más ambiciosas en términos de sostenibilidad, y, con ello también, en una ciudad a la que mirar desde el ámbito regional, estatal, europeo e internacional.
El Sello de Misión es, ante todo, un reconocimiento de la finalización con éxito del proceso de Acuerdo Climático de Ciudad. Ese documento se ha sometido en los últimos meses a un exhaustivo control de integridad por parte de la Plataforma de Misiones (NetZeroCities) y, a continuación, en abril de 2023, se presentó oficialmente a la Comisión Europea para su revisión. Tras proceder al análisis de su Acuerdo Climático, y tras consultar al Consejo de Misiones (Mission´s Board) y al Grupo de Propietarios de Misiones de la Comisión (Commission´s Mission Owners Group), se ha concedido a Vitoria-Gasteiz el Sello de Misión
De entre las más de 370 ciudades europeas que lo intentaron, en abril de 2022 Vitoria-Gasteiz fue elegida una de las 100 Ciudades Misión. Desde entonces, ha estado trabajando en el diseño y desarrollo de su Acuerdo Climático de Ciudad (Climate City Contract), un paso fundamental en la participación en esta Misión europea. 
La Misión Europea de 100 Ciudades Inteligentes y Climáticamente Neutras para 2030 en la que toma parte Vitoria-Gasteiz tiene como objetivo conseguir 100 ciudades inteligentes y neutras desde el punto de vista climático para el año 2030, y garantizar que estas ciudades actúen como centros de experimentación e innovación para permitir que todas las ciudades europeas sigan su ejemplo para 2050. Para conseguir estos objetivos la Misión de las Ciudades Inteligentes y Climáticamente neutras implicará a las autoridades locales, los ciudadanos, las empresas, los inversores y las autoridades regionales y nacionales.

Files 01 to 04 - Hermosillo on a Human Scale: A Diversified, Innovative, and Sustainable City

The Emerging and Sustainable Cities Initiative (ESC) in Hermosillo, Sonora, is a comprehensive, interdisciplinary urban study that identifies and prioritizes interventions in areas such as energy, mobility and transportation, fiscal sustainability, and water. Its goal is to promote sustainability in urban planning and growth. The initiative was developed by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for emerging cities in Latin America. The North American Development Bank (NADBank) partnered with the IDB to launch the program in Mexican border communities.

File 05 - Green Infrastructure Manual (Developed by the Municipality of Hermosillo)

General Objective: To guide the design and decision-making process for incorporating Green Infrastructure (G.I.) in Mexican municipalities through technical design guidelines at the micro-scale level (techniques and technologies) and a methodology for application at the macro-scale level (urban basin and sub-basin scale), achieved through strategic planning, participatory management, and adaptation to local ecosystem conditions.

Specific Objective at the Micro Scale: To develop technical design specifications for G.I. based on roadway categories, built environments, and the urbanization of areas where green infrastructure is implemented.

Specific Objective at the Macro Scale: To establish a foundation for developing a methodology that supports the design and planning of G.I. at the scale of urban basins, sub-basins, neighborhoods, and cities.

File 06 - Advanced Electric Transport and Sustainable Mobilities (TEAMS)

The Letter of Intent for TEAMS outlines the commitment and interest of the involved parties to collaborate on developing and implementing advanced electric transportation and sustainable mobility solutions. This document serves as a formal expression of intent to work together, detailing the general terms and objectives that will guide future actions, such as improving electric transport infrastructure, promoting sustainable urban mobility, and fostering technological innovation. While not legally binding, it sets the stage for more detailed agreements and strategic partnerships related to the TEAMS initiative.

Municipal Urban Development Program 
Unrestricted link: https://boletinoficial.sonora.gob.mx/images/boletines/2023/09/2023CCXII21III.pdf

The Municipal Urban Development Program is a technical and regulatory document created by authorities, specialists, and the broader community. The Municipal Development Plan 2025-2027 focuses on generating tangible, measurable, and evaluable results. This document incorporates a collection of proposals and aspirations from the community, organized around five major strategic fronts. These fronts outline challenges, strategies, and action lines that emerged from the efforts of citizen transition committees and all who participated in collaborative spaces to define the direction of public decision-making:

sierra, rodeada por volcanes activos (MPA-AECI, s.f.).

La Administración Municipal 2024-2027 se ha incorporado a la red de Gobiernos Locales para la Sostenibilidad (ICLEI) con el propósito de acceder a asesoría técnica especializada, programas de capacitación y referencias internacionales de políticas públicas que han demostrado resultados tangibles en otras ciudades y regiones. Esta vinculación permitirá fortalecer la toma de decisiones y afrontar con mayor capacidad los desafíos ambientales presentes y futuros en nuestro municipio.

Con base en este acompañamiento estratégico, el Ayuntamiento impulsa diversas iniciativas prioritarias:

• Implementación del Plan de Acción Climática Municipal (PACMUN): Se trabaja en la adopción y consolidación de este instrumento, que orientará las políticas locales de mitigación y adaptación al cambio climático. El PACMUN permitirá identificar fuentes de emisiones, evaluar riesgos climáticos y definir acciones puntuales para reducir la vulnerabilidad de la población y de la infraestructura urbana.

• Fortalecimiento del Programa de Ecología Táctica: Este programa se está robusteciendo para ejecutar intervenciones rápidas, de bajo costo y alto impacto en el territorio municipal. Su objetivo es prevenir riesgos ambientales, mejorar el entorno urbano y operar estrategias que fomenten la participación comunitaria y la recuperación de espacios públicos mediante soluciones verdes y sostenibles.

• Visión estratégica hacia el Plan San Luis 2050: La administración impulsa programas y acciones que sirvan como cimientos para una agenda ambiental de largo plazo. La visión al 2050 busca encaminar al municipio hacia un desarrollo sostenible, resiliente y competitivo, mediante políticas que promuevan el uso eficiente de recursos, la transición energética, la protección de los ecosistemas y la mejora en la calidad de vida de las y los ciudadanos.

Con estas líneas de acción, la Administración Municipal reafirma su compromiso con la sostenibilidad y la resiliencia climática, aprovechando la experiencia global de CDP, ICLEI entre otras instituciones para adecuarla al contexto local y generar beneficios directos para San Luis Potosí.

Davao City continues to strengthen its climate action agenda through the integration of mitigation, adaptation, and resilience measures across local plans and programs. The City's Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) 2024-2026, together with complementary sectoral plans such as the Comprehensive Land Use Plan (CLUP) 2019-2028, Forest Land Use Plan, Ecological Solid Waste Management Plan, and Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Plan, provide a strong policy framework for addressing climate risks.

The city has also aligned its greenhouse gas emissions reduction target with the WWF One Planet City Challenge (OPCC) framework, committing to a net zero target by 2050. This reflects Davao's commitment to go beyond national contributions and position itself as a model for sustainable and resilient urban development in the Philippines.

Davao City continues to face challenges such as energy poverty, food deserts in remote barangays, and limited infrastructure for climate data consolidation. Nonetheless, the city government is pursuing strategies to address these issues, including renewable energy expansion, sustainable mobility, and investments in resilient agriculture and food systems.

Iskandar Malaysia is a special economic zone and the main southern development corridor in Johor, Malaysia. It was established on November 8, 2006, with the aim of strengthening Malaysia's economic competitiveness and improving the quality of life for its citizens. The region is strategically located as the southern gateway to Malaysia and neighboring Singapore, facilitating transboundary economic activity and attracting investments of MYR453 billion / EUR91 billion (September 2024). 

 
Iskandar Malaysia also serves as a foundation for the newer Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) initiative, which aims to deepen economic integration and collaboration between Johor and Singapore. Strategic areas within Iskandar Malaysia—such as Pengerang and Iskandar Puteri, including Forest City—are being proposed as key zones within this cross-border economic partnership. Iskandar Malaysia Regional Authority (IRDA) is currently in the midst of collaborating with 5 PBTs to produce a GHG Inventory for the year 2022 and 2023. This GHG emissions reporting objectives is to continuously track and monitor GHG emissions for Iskandar Malaysia as part of low carbon society blueprint monitoring framework cycle. The GHG Inventory will be 'BASIC' reporting covering Stationary Energy, Transportation and Waste and will include materiality assessment and data readiness for Pengerang's Industrial Processes and Product Use (IPPU). IRDA is currently preparing the new Term of Reference (TOR) for Green House Gas Inventory for Iskandar Malaysia and Pengerang (area for JS- SEZ). This is to monitor GHG emissions intensity and review the progress against GHG targets set for 2025. This GHG reporting is a science-based target setting and crucial towards enabling Iskandar Malaysia to achieve net-zero target by 2050 and to be in line with national aspiration of a carbon neutral nation.

The first part of the sustainable net-zero trilogy was to sign the 'Climate Emergency Declaration' in January 2021 and proposed the 'Sustainable 168 Goal Strategy', of which 'the first goal' was to build Taichung into a coal-free city and '6'covered the renewable energy utilization rate reaching 20% in 2030. The new lease-purchase manufacturers in the industrial zones within the city's jurisdiction must install photovoltaics on 50% of the roof area, the average annual concentration of PM2.5 in 2030 to 12 micrograms, and the proportion of electric buses increasing. to 40%, the growth rate of electric motorcycles to 200%, and the reduction of greenhouse gases in 2030 compared to the base year (2005) to reach 30%; the last '8' goals are the United Nations' goals 7, 9, and 11 to promote sustainable development. goals 12, 13, 14, 15 and 17, hoping to build a sustainable city in line with international trends and fight climate change together with major cities around the world.

The second part, '2021 Taichung City Voluntary Inspection Report'was released in September 2021. We injected 'sunshine, air, water' into the environmental, economic, social and other policy development strategies, and comprehensively promote 17 sustainable development goals and 103 Indicators and 106 plans.

The trilogy released the goal of '2050 Taichung City Net-Zero Carbon Emission Path' in 2022, outlines 6 key strategies and 20 zero-carbon paths, and continues to strive to improve air pollution and reduce carbon emissions through energy transformation and the promotion of various departments and is to build the vision towards net-zero carbon emissions in 2050.

Oulu is the largest owner of municipal forests in Finland. We own approximately 19,500 hectares (ha) of forestry land. Of the forestry land, about 3,200 ha are poorly productive forest lands and unproductive land, peat bogs, wide power lines, roads, etc. Forests and bogs are protected in an area of approx. 1,300 ha (including valuable habitats according to the Forest Act), which is approx. 7% of the area of forestry land. The forests produce approximately 40,000 m3 of lumber for factories and sawmills annually. In addition to this, logging residue collected from the urban area is used for energy production in thermal power plants, mainly in Toppila. A part of the twigs are turned into mulch for the flower beds and shrubs in the city's parks and surface material for nature trails. The current carbon storage of the city's forests is 2.7 million tonnes of CO2.- The city has a Forest Management Plan for 2024-2033. Reykjavik city transitioned to renewable energy for both power production and geothermal central heating half a century ago. Thanks to this historical switch to renewable energy, a mix of geothermal and hydropower for both electricity production and central heating, Reykjavik has a unique emissions profile where most of the emissions come from transportation. 
Reykjavik City´s work on Climate issues the next years to come will be focused on the Climate City Contract with the support of NetZero Cities. The main strategic priorities in the commitments of the Climate City Contract: 
1.	Mobility, focus on change in travel modes and strengthening the infrastructure for public transport, pedestrians and cyclists. 
2.	Energy transition of the car fleet and at the port of Reykjavík with carbon neutral produced energy 
3.	Waste and circular economy, including increased recycling by the private sector and individuals. 
4.	Building sector. The City has ambitious goals for the development of residential housing. It is therefore important that this development has as little impact on the climate and environment as possible. 
5.	Just transition -Various ways to ensure a just transition are already in place at the City of Reykjavík and are described in detail in the Action Plan. 
The CCC includes 15 actions, including 2 adaptations actions.

The commitment to the Low Carbon agenda as a cross-cutting theme within the City Plan has meant that work to effectively mitigate and adapt to climate change continues to remain a significant key priority in Sunderland. Partner organisations are continuing to develop their own Low Carbon Action Plans in line with the seven strategic priorities of the citywide Low Carbon Framework. To continue its leadership within the city, the Council is has also developed a more robust version of its own Low Carbon Action Plan, which was approved by Cabinet in July 2022, and is reviewed annual by the Council's Senior Manager and the Council Low Carbon Task Group to ensure focus and delivery, and is available at https://www.mysunderland.co.uk/media/27384/Sunderland-Low-Carbon-Action-Plan-2022/pdf/oce22135_Sunderland_Low_Carbon_Action_Plan_A4_2022.pdf?m=637988302419030000. This has been enabled through greater and consistent cross-organisational working since January 2021, through the Council's Carbon Task Group, and an increased understanding of data. The Council's Carbon Task Group meets regularly and focus on actions for the year ahead, whilst supporting each other to collaborate and tackle challenges together.
 
To continue to increase engagement and embed climate action, Sunderland City Council is participating in the UK100 Local Climate Engagement Programme, which is a partnership with Involve, the Democratic Society, Shared Future and Climate Outreach and is working with local authorities to deliver high-quality public engagement projects on climate policy in a way that benefits both them and their local communities. Sunderland's project is focussing on public engagement around sustainability travel behaviours and has provided training to approximately 20 members of staff. Elected members have also been made aware of this initiative to further embed positive climate action engagement.

Sunderland City Council has used the feedback from the 2021-2024 CDP disclosures to assess weaker areas (adaptation goals, transport, waste and food) and has included a greater focus on activity in these areas during the last year.
 
In 2024 and up to June 2025, Sunderland City Council has coordinated and facilitated a range of 'partner' deep dive sessions with other key organisations represented on the Shadow Board. These are identifying areas for deeper collaboration (data sharing, communications, tree planting, decarbonisation of assets inc. fleet etc) and specifically during 2025, Adaptation planning. The Shadow Board partners have also formed a communications officer group which brings together leads from all Shadow Board members to work on citywide messaging and key sustainability campaigns.

North East Combined Authority:
The North East Combined Authority was formed on 7 May 2024. Led by an Elected Mayor and Cabinet and covers the seven local authority areas of County Durham, Gateshead, Newcastle, North Tyneside, Northumberland, South Tyneside and Sunderland. 

The purpose is to champion the full potential of our region. Collaborating with our partners and local authorities, creating a better way of life by connecting communities, giving people the skills to succeed, and improving wellbeing for all, so that the North East is recognised as an outstanding place to live, work, visit and invest.

The North east Combined Authority has five commitments.

A fairer North East. We'll help people thrive with aspirational jobs, new skills, and better homes, improving quality of life for everyone. We'll create confidence in the North East by reducing inequalities and improving health.
 
A greener North East. We'll take inspiration from our industrial heritage and unique mix of urban areas, countryside, coastline and rivers, to nurture our natural resources - creating green jobs, sustainable industry, and clean energy.

A connected North East. We'll get behind businesses so they can improve productivity and connectivity. With better local transport networks and digital infrastructures, the North East will have a global reach, becoming the go-to place for innovative ideas and real-world results.

An international North East. Building on our economic strength, and championing our heritage, culture, arts and sports, we'll drive the region's ambition to continually attract visitors and investment.

A successful North East. Together, we'll speak with one voice, and define our own future, cultivating the talent, skills and innovation that will help grow our existing economy, becoming green industry leaders and a cultural destination - making the North East one of the best places to live, work, and invest.”

The Council Senior Manager for Low Carbon and Sustainable Regeneration works closely with their counterparts in each of the seven regional LAs, to ensure partnership working. During 2025, the focus has been in relation to green investment and skills; domestic retrofitting, decarbonisation support to businesses and community organisations as well as aligning plans and strategies and carbon accounting practices. The regional working has also enabled Sunderland to secure funding and investment to introduce Solar PV into schools in Sunderland via the mayoral Support fund as well as tapping into Great British Energy funding support (see 9.2).
Additional information relating to working with the Voluntary and Community Sector:VCS Networks are in place in the city, Organisations working at grass roots are consulted during the development and delivery of Area Investment Plans and commissioned to deliver support services within communities, increasing opportunities for social value-added. The views and input of all sectors of the community are considered, and many of the groups working in the most deprived neighbourhoods are contributing to changing behaviours to address climate change. SVSA are a member of the 2030 Shadow Board. 

Sunderland was an early adopter of infrastructure to support use of electric vehicles. As part of the North East Plugged-In Places programme (2010-2012), charging stations were introduced across the city. Further EV infrastructure is being rolled out across Sunderland, including new facilities in Holmeside in the city centre, which will be open from October 2024, and at municipal car parks and at key destinations. In Sunderland, as of April 2025, 1,113 chargepoints were installed between 2014-2024 through the Electric Vehicle Homecharge Scheme and 253 sockets were installed through the Workplace Charging Scheme. In 2019 Sunderland had the highest number of EV charging points per vehicle licence holder in the whole of the UK (1 for every 1460 drivers). As of July 2025, Sunderland has 128 publicly available charging points per 100,000 people, which is the highest amount in the region. The city also boasts the country's first rapid charging electric vehicle station which offers four 50 kW fast chargers and two 175kW fast chargers that are enabled for 350 kW charging (the fastest available nationally). SCC has recently installed further rapid hubs and are progressing a pilot on-street charge-point scheme. A pilot scheme delivering cross pavement charging channels to support residents is also being delivered by SCC. Encouraging greater use of low emission vehicles also reflects Sunderland's leading role as part of the UK's low carbon economy. Sunderland-based advanced manufacturing businesses are playing a key role in the decarbonisation of transport.

WWF One Planet Challenge : Sunderland was delighted to be named Global Winner of WWF's One Planet City Challenge in 2024, alongside the city of Istanbul. 
One Planet City Challenge is the largest and longest-running climate challenge for cities in the world, with 359 cities from 48 countries taking part this year alone.
Designed to highlight leading examples of climate mitigation and adaptation from cities around the world, Sunderland was selected as a global winner after evaluation by a high-level jury of urban experts from a wide range of organisations including the World Economic Forum, Global Covenant of Mayors and World Bank.
Sunderland and Istanbul were the frontrunners based on the evaluation of their reported climate data compared to other participating cities
Feedback from Kristen Schuit, Director General from WWF International stated “In a world full of many difficult challenges, it is really inspiring to witness the results of cities in action, and their extraordinary potential to reverse negative trends. Thanks to ambitious climate leadership and determination, Sunderland (and Istanbul) have become stellar examples of cities that aim to create more sustainable places for us to live and thrive - while striving to respect the ecological boundaries of our planet.”
OPCC cities globally are showing the world what can be achieved in sustainability at a time when that goal has never been more critical. As global winners, Sunderland and Istanbul will be held up as examples to towns and cities the world over of how to commit to meaningful and ambitious climate action.  
The jury was impressed by Sunderland's “ambitious, multi-dimensional, and well-balanced approach to climate action across all sectors.” The judges also reserved special praise for Sunderland's “innovative “Shadow Board” which highlights inclusive decision-making and offers a model for other cities to replicate.”
Being shortlisted was a real achievement but to win demonstrates just how hard everyone in Sunderland, are working to help us achieve our ambitious mission of becoming carbon neutral as a city by 2040.

As the previous question from CDP 2024, “8.3 Does your jurisdiction have a strategy for reducing emissions from consumption of the most relevant goods and services?” appears to not be included in CDP 2025, our prepared response has been integrated into the disclosure where possible, in case the question being missed from the CDP questionnaire was an error?

Com o intuito de fornecer um contexto adicional relevante para a análise desta jurisdição, informamos que o Município de Palmas tem avançado significativamente na estruturação de sua política climática. Atualmente, a gestão está focada na consolidação e elaboração do Plano de Ação Climática (PAC) do município.
Este esforço é respaldado pela recente criação da Diretoria de Mudanças Climáticas e Cerrado Amazônico, um eixo organizacional estabelecido este ano e dedicado especificamente à pauta climática. Adicionalmente, o município está em processo de preenchimento e atualização de seu inventário de emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (GEE), um passo fundamental para basear o PAC em dados robustos.
É importante ressaltar que a preocupação de Palmas com a agenda climática não é recente. O município instituiu sua Política Municipal de Mudanças Climáticas em 2003, por meio da Lei Nº 1.182, que já previa a regulação de projetos nas áreas florestal e energética para mitigação das emissões. Esta base legal foi fortalecida pelo Plano Diretor Participativo (Lei Complementar N° 400/2018), que estabelece a 'adaptação e a mitigação dos impactos relacionados às mudanças climáticas' como um de seus princípios fundamentais (Art. 5º).
A elaboração do PAC se baseia em diagnósticos aprofundados já realizados, como o 'Plano de Ação Palmas Sustentável', desenvolvido no âmbito da Iniciativa Cidades Emergentes e Sustentáveis (ICES). Este plano identificou áreas críticas para a sustentabilidade da cidade, incluindo mobilidade, uso do solo e gestão de resíduos sólidos, temas diretamente ligados às emissões de GEE.
Estudos específicos de mitigação e vulnerabilidade também fornecem a base técnica para o PAC. O inventário de GEE de Palmas aponta o setor de transportes como a principal fonte de emissões. Por outro lado, os estudos de vulnerabilidade indicam que o município está exposto a riscos como ondas de calor e eventos de chuvas extremas que podem levar a alagamentos.
Diversas ações para enfrentar esses desafios já estão em andamento ou planejadas, como o Plano de Arborização Urbana, que visa, entre outros, a melhoria do microclima e a redução das ilhas de calor. O Plano Diretor também prevê a implementação de um Sistema Municipal de Infraestrutura Verde (SisMIV) para propiciar maior capacidade de adaptação aos ecossistemas urbanos e rurais.
Em suma, o município de Palmas está em um momento estratégico de consolidação de sua governança climática, com uma base legal, diagnósticos técnicos e um novo arranjo institucional que demonstram o compromisso da gestão em avançar de forma estruturada e informada na agenda de enfrentamento às mudanças climáticas, em alinhamento com a Política Nacional sobre Mudança do Clima (Lei Nº 12.187/2009).

Em 2024 Guimarães vence o título Capital Verde Europeia 2026 e obtém o selo da Missão Cidades (Mission label) vendo reconhecido, pela Comissão Europeia, o seu compromisso com a sustentabilidade ambiental e com a neutralidade climática até 2030. Para além da Missão das Cidades, Guimarães integra a Missão dos Oceanos, a Missão dos Solos e a Missão da Adaptação. Estes reconhecimentos e compromissos resultam de uma estratégia estabelecida há mais de 10 anos, da qual faz parte o Sistema Ambiental Integrado que relaciona 7 áreas de indicadores ambientais e um indicador de democracia participativa; transversal a todas as áreas. Para além de serem estudados e relacionados, de uma forma multidisciplinar e transversal, estes indicadores são também monitorizados em termos de impactes e co benefícios; incluindo as questões da saúde e bem-estar dos cidadãos, e de desenvolvimento económico sustentado. O Plano de Ação Climática 2030 é monitorizado de acordo com um complexo sistema de indicadores de performance que incluem: indicadores de curto prazo (taxa de implementação), de médio prazo (resultados tangíveis) e de longo prazo (impacte). Cada uma das áreas estratégicas para o clima, apresenta, igualmente, um conjunto de indicadores de monitorização específicos. Refira-se apenas a título de exemplo: a Mobilidade com 115 indicadores de execução, os Resíduos e Economia circular: indicadores da metodologia Circular Cities and Regions Initiative (CCRI) da Comissão Europeia, a Natureza e Biodiversidade com indicadores incluídos no Plano De Ação Local Para a Biodiversidade 2030. Para além destes indicadores de execução, foi estabelecido um conselho municipal de acompanhamento e monitorização que inclui, partidos políticos, associações, NGO's, entidades regionais e nacionais com competências relacionadas com o Ambiente e Clima (ex. CCDR, Agência Portuguesa do Ambiente, entre outras). O primeiro Relatório de Execução 2025, está em vias de conclusão para submissão à comissão. Este relatório compreende a taxa de execução das medidas de adaptação e mitigação bem como, uma análise de SWOT para identificação de constrangimentos e novas oportunidades. Adicionalmente, no âmbito do Green City Accord (GCA), estão consignadas metas intermédias para 2026 com KPI's de execução nas cinco áreas consignadas pelo GCA: Ar, Ruído, Água, natureza e Biodiversidade e Resíduos. Realce-se a importância das metas intermédias, definidas para 2026, com vista à obtenção de uma taxa de execução na ordem dos 100%, em 2030. No âmbito da Missão de Adaptação às Alterações Climáticas, Guimarães tem desenvolvido e implementado um conjunto de medidas baseadas na Natureza que contribuem para aumentar a resiliência do território. Com o DISTENDER, as sinergias e os indicadores de compromisso para a mitigação/adaptação são integrados num sistema de apoio à decisão. 
No âmbito da Missão para a neutralidade climática refira-se que o Contrato Climático para a neutralidade climática em 2030 incorpora um plano de ação e de investimentos com medidas concretas e indicadores de performance que visam a neutralidade climática em 2030. Refira-se que foi também desenvolvido o Pacto climático com o objetivo de mobilizar o setor privado para esta jornada climática. De forma a monitorizar o contributo deste setor (nomeadamente da componente industrial que é cluster que mais contribui para as emissões globais), o Laboratório da Paisagem de Guimarães, em situações específicas, disponibiliza aos subscritores o cálculo da PEGADA Carbónica. Os resultados são posteriormente analisados e estudados em termos de impacto para as emissões globais.
A Pegada Ecológica Municipal para análise da performance municipal e o Estudo das Perceções e dos Hábitos Ambientais dos Habitantes de Guimarães são também instrumentos de monitorização que visam a análise da efetividade das medidas em termos de alterações comportamentais. Estes dois instrumentos são implementados a cada cinco anos. Em 2025, está a decorrer a terceira edição do Estudo das Perceções e dos Hábitos Ambientais dos Habitantes de Guimarães. 
Depois de ter sido, por três anos consecutivos o Município Eco XXI mais sustentável de Portugal, o município tem apostado na transmissão das políticas de desenvolvimento sustentável para uma escala contextual menor. Neste sentido, e de forma continuada, são várias as freguesias que têm aceite o desafio de obterem a certificação de Eco-Freguesias. Esta iniciativa da ABAE, visa incrementar o desenvolvimento sustentável à escala local procurando envolver os cidadãos em geral, e os dirigentes das juntas de freguesias em particular, na construção de uma sustentabilidade participada. Em 2025, Guimarães continua a reforçar o compromisso com o desenvolvimento sustentável a nível local, com 14 freguesias a conquistar o Galardão Bandeira Verde Eco-Freguesias XXI. 
O projeto “Desporto Carbono Zero” é um projeto pioneiro em Guimarães e a nível nacional e o seu principal objetivo do projeto é a criação de um plano de sustentabilidade ambiental que contribua para a diminuição da pegada ecológica dos clubes desportivos, partindo de um diagnóstico inicial. A iniciativa foi desenhada para incentivar os 55 clubes desportivos do município, num total de mais de 7 mil atletas, a criarem planos de sustentabilidade, a gerirem a sua performance ambiental através de uma plataforma, e a orientar as atividades do clube para a concretização dos objetivos do desenvolvimento sustentável 2030. Esta iniciativa está a ser concretizada através do acompanhamento técnico especializado na área de sustentabilidade ambiental; capacitação e formação da gestão do clube na área de sustentabilidade ambiental levada a cabo pelo Laboratório da Paisagem de Guimarães. No âmbito do programa cultura carbono zero, a atividade cultural também está a ser monitorizada. As entidades participadas têm também desenvolvido o seu plano de ação com indicadores de desempenho ambiental.
Guimarães é líder nacional instalação de Painéis Solares para autoconsumo, demonstrando o compromisso de todos os vimaranenses, famílias e empresas, com a transição energética e a sustentabilidade ambiental. Neste momento e no âmbito do projeto Piloto da Missão cidades - Bairro C - Guimarães está a desenvolver a sua primeira comunidade de energia com intervenção do município com vista a fornecer energia limpa a uma parte dos edifícios do bairro C, localizado no Património UNESCO mais conhecido como COUROS. Guimarães apostou também na implementação de medidas construtivas eficientes e no âmbito da estratégia NZEB+20, os novos edifícios públicos incorporam já medidas de autossustentabilidade e neutralidade climática.

A estratégia de sustentabilidade do Município de Braga está centrada numa abordagem holística e integrada ao desenvolvimento sustentável, com um forte foco no combate às alterações climáticas e na promoção de práticas sustentáveis em diversas áreas. O Plano Estratégico para o Desenvolvimento Sustentável de Braga 2030 define as diretrizes e ações prioritárias para tornar Braga mais verde, inovadora e resiliente. Este plano foi desenvolvido em colaboração com a comunidade local e parceiros estratégicos, promovendo a participação ativa de todas as partes interessadas.

O Relatório de Sustentabilidade é uma ferramenta crucial para a monitorização e transparência das iniciativas de Braga em prol da sustentabilidade. O município aderiu a normas internacionais, como a Global Reporting Initiative e o Greenhouse Gas Protocol, para garantir a medição rigorosa dos seus progressos, tanto no nível operacional como comunitário. Este relatório reflete o alinhamento das políticas de Braga com os Objetivos de Desenvolvimento Sustentável (ODS) das Nações Unidas, demonstrando um compromisso claro com a Agenda 2030.

O Município de Braga participa ativamente em redes internacionais relacionadas com as alterações climáticas e o desenvolvimento sustentável, tais como o ICLEI - Local Governments for Sustainability e a EuroCities. Estas redes facilitam a troca de conhecimentos e melhores práticas, bem como o desenvolvimento de soluções inovadoras para os desafios climáticos e urbanos. A participação no Green City Accord e no Pacto dos Autarcas para o Clima e a Energia reforça o empenho de Braga em reduzir as emissões de carbono e em adaptar a cidade às alterações climáticas, promovendo a energia limpa, a mobilidade sustentável e a economia circular.

Em síntese, apesar do foco específico em medidas contra as alterações climáticas, a estratégia de Braga vai além, abordando áreas como a mobilidade, o urbanismo sustentável, a gestão da água e resíduos, a saúde e o bem-estar da comunidade, e a descarbonização da cidade. Este compromisso global posicionou Braga entre as 8 cidades candidatas ao título de Capital Verde Europeia da União Europeia.

According to Article 3 of Taiwan's Electricity Act, the analysis, formulation, and promotion of electricity policies fall under the jurisdiction of the central government. Taiwan's electricity supply is planned and managed by the Taiwan Power Company (Taipower), a state-owned enterprise authorized by the central government. Taipower operates power plants across the country and distributes electricity to all cities and counties in a unified manner.

As such, responses to questions 4.1, 7.1, and 9.2 of this questionnaire—regarding electricity mix restructuring, renewable energy targets, and implementation progress—must be based on the central government's energy transition schedule. Likewise, the medium- and long-term reduction targets in question 6 must align with national energy transition plans. According to the current national roadmap, the emission factor of electricity is set to decrease to 0.424 kg CO₂e/kWh by 2025, and further to 0.319 kg CO₂e/kWh by 2030 (compared to 0.559 kg CO₂e/kWh in 2005). By 2050, the renewable energy share in the national electricity mix is expected to reach 60% to 70%.

New Taipei City continues to actively collaborate with the central government in promoting decentralized renewable energy installations, including geothermal power development, solar photovoltaic deployment, and biogas power generation. The city government has also identified potential public and private sites to facilitate citizen participation through subsidies and regulatory mechanisms. However, because electricity in Taiwan is centrally distributed, the outcomes of these local policies are reflected nationally, rather than solely in New Taipei City's GHG inventory. In addition, energy poverty and energy accessibility fall under the scope of national social protection policies. The central government regulates electricity pricing nationwide and has established an Electricity Price Stabilization Fund in accordance with Article 9 of the Electricity Act.
